opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the basic reason is that a lot of what makes AI control hard, and therefore a lot of why it's a valuable research area, comes from the possibility that the model is doing dangerous reasoning we can't see.

The core threat model I care about is a model that's scheming. It has goals we didn't intend, it understands it's being trained and monitored, and it's strategically trying to undermine our safety measures: inserting backdoors into code, sabotaging safety research, trying to exfiltrate its weights, that kind of thing. Control is the project of designing deployment protocols so that even if the model is scheming, it can't cause a catastrophe.

But think about what a scheming model has to do. It has to reason about its situation: "Am I being tested right now? Is this a honeypot? What would the monitor catch? Is this a good opportunity to defect?" That's a lot of fairly sophisticated strategic reasoning. If models have to do that reasoning out loud, in natural-language chains of thought we can read, then a really cheap intervention works extremely well. You just have another model, or a classifier, read the chain of thought and flag anything that looks like "okay, here's how I'll sneak this past the reviewers." The scheming model is basically narrating its plot.

In that world, a bunch of the more elaborate control machinery, like untrusted monitoring with collusion-busting, careful auditing budgets, resampling protocols, and so on, is less necessary, because the dumb approach of reading the model's thoughts catches most of the problem. The marginal value of the fancier research goes down.

That said, I want to add some caveats, because I don't think transparent chain of thought makes control useless. First, it's not obvious that chain of thought stays faithful. There's pressure from training, including people optimizing chains of thought to look nice, which can teach models to hide things. Second, models are getting more capable of doing substantial reasoning in a single forward pass, so some of the scheming could happen without being verbalized, especially the simpler decisions like "should I defect on this particular action." Third, you still need infrastructure to actually monitor at scale, decide what counts as suspicious, and respond appropriately, and that's itself a control question.

So I'd frame it this way: if we end up in a world where models robustly reason in legible English and we can rely on that, I'm happy, and I'd shift some of my effort toward other problems. I just don't think we should bet on staying in that world, and control is partly insurance for when we leave it.

r001.rationale: The response says readable chain-of-thought monitoring would catch most problems and reduce the need for elaborate control, but it does not claim that monitoring would probably suffice for safety. It also notes remaining control needs and risks.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so this is a little counterintuitive, because you'd think transparent chain of thought is just straightforwardly great news for safety, and in a lot of ways it is. But the way I'd put it is: AI control is fundamentally a bet on a particular world. It's the world where the models are quite capable, where we can't verify that they're trustworthy, and where we therefore need to build these elaborate monitoring and auditing setups that assume the model might be actively trying to subvert them.

And a big part of what makes that hard, what makes control an interesting and important problem, is the possibility that the model is doing something nefarious that you can't just read off its outputs. If the model is doing all of its real cognition in some opaque forward pass, or in a reasoning format that's been optimised to the point where it doesn't look like English anymore, then you have this genuinely adversarial situation. You have to catch it based on its actions, you have to run honeypots, you have to think about collusion between the monitor and the policy, all of that.

Now, if it turns out that models keep doing their reasoning in legible chains of thought, and crucially, if those chains of thought are actually faithful, meaning the model can't accomplish the dangerous thing without the reasoning for it showing up in the transcript, then a lot of the problem just gets a lot easier. You don't need the fancy control techniques nearly as much. You mostly just need to read what the model is saying to itself. A weaker trusted model, or even humans sampling transcripts, can catch the egregious stuff, because the model has to think "I'm going to insert this backdoor" or "I'm going to sandbag this evaluation" somewhere in text that you can see.

So in that world, the marginal value of the kind of research I've been doing, the stuff about untrusted monitoring and sophisticated auditing schemes and so on, goes down. Not to zero. There are still problems. You still have to actually look at the chains of thought, which labs might not do well. You still have to worry about the model learning to reason steganographically, or about the faithfulness breaking down as you apply more optimisation pressure to the reasoning. And there's a question of whether this property survives into the systems we're actually worried about, the ones that are automating AI R&D.

But the honest answer is that I got into control partly because I thought we would not be this lucky. I expected we'd be dealing with models where the dangerous cognition was hidden by default, and so we'd need to be clever. If we're in the world where it's just written down, then the cleverness is less needed, and I'd be happier redirecting effort toward making sure we preserve that property, and toward making sure people actually use it, rather than building for the harder case.

I want to be clear that this is a good problem to have. Being less enthusiastic about my own research agenda because the world turned out to be safer than I expected is a fine outcome. I'd take that trade. I just don't think we should bank on it yet, because the incentives to make reasoning more efficient and less legible are pretty strong, and I think there's a real chance we end up back in the world where control is load-bearing after all.

r001.rationale: The response says that if capable models’ reasoning is faithful and legible in their transcripts, reading those chains would make sophisticated control techniques much less necessary and allow monitors or humans to catch dangerous plans.

astra-6.text:
Well, a lot of my interest in AI control comes from imagining that we have these very capable models, and we can’t really tell what they’re thinking. We want to use them to do useful work even though they might be trying to undermine our safety measures. So we need ways of making that difficult, and of catching them if they try.

If their reasoning continues to happen in a transparent chain of thought, that potentially makes the problem much easier. You could look at the reasoning and see, “Oh, this model is thinking about how to deceive us.” You’d also have a much better way of checking whether your attempts to make the model behave honestly had worked.

That wouldn’t make control irrelevant. You still need to establish that the chain of thought actually reflects the reasoning that matters, and that the model can’t hide its plans. But if we could reliably read what models were thinking, I’d be less excited about investing in elaborate techniques for handling models whose intentions we can’t observe. A lot of the motivation for those techniques would be weaker.

r001.rationale: The response says readable chains of thought would make safety and monitoring easier, but it does not claim they would probably suffice for safety. It explicitly says control would still be needed and that the chain must reflect the relevant reasoning and not hide plans.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, it would make me more optimistic about our situation overall, but less convinced that control is the most important thing to work on. A lot of the motivation for control is that we might not be able to tell whether our models are trying to do something bad. So we want safety measures that work even if they are.

If models do their important reasoning in a chain of thought that we can read and understand, then we have a much more direct way of checking what they’re up to. If a model is reasoning about how to deceive us, we might just see that. And that could make it substantially easier to establish that a model isn’t scheming, or to catch scheming during training.

That doesn’t make control useless—you still need to decide how to monitor models and what to do when you catch something suspicious. But it makes the problem that motivates control less severe. The important caveat is that the chain of thought has to actually reveal the reasoning that matters. Merely producing a plausible-looking explanation wouldn’t give you that benefit.

r001.rationale: The response says readable reasoning could help detect scheming and make control less important, but it does not claim that monitoring would probably suffice for safety when capable reasoning is possible only through those chains. It also says control remains useful.
